name: Standard Scramble

waypoints.name: Libby Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FS Road 4340-750; roadside parking for ~10 cars, no facilities — start of Libby Creek Trail #415.
waypoints.directions: Drive Libby Creek Road to its end at FS Road 4340-750, where the Libby Lake Trailhead — also called the Libby Creek Trailhead — sits at about 4,400 ft. Parking is roadside for roughly ten cars, with no facilities. No fee or pass is required here. Libby Creek Trail No. 415 starts from the road end and heads southwest into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness.

waypoints.name: Burn-zone spring
waypoints.note: Reliable spring 0.6 mile into the patchwork 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire burn scar; last easy water before the wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: Follow Libby Creek Trail No. 415 southwest through mixed conifer, crossing small tributaries on logs or rocks, about 1.4 miles to a spring in the patchy burn scar.

waypoints.name: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness boundary
waypoints.note: Signed wilderness entry 0.3 mile past the spring; trail continues climbing through mixed burned/live forest.
waypoints.directions: Continue climbing on the trail about 0.3 mile to the signed Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness boundary.

waypoints.name: North Fork Libby Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford the North Fork of Libby Creek; an established campsite on the far bank is the last reliable water before the cabin.
waypoints.directions: Keep on Trail No. 415 through mixed burned and live forest to the ford of the North Fork of Libby Creek, with an established campsite on the far bank. This is the last reliable water.

waypoints.name: Historic trapper's cabin
waypoints.note: Decaying cabin where the scramble route leaves Libby Creek Trail; a faint boot path angles right (west) into the trees toward Hoodoo.
waypoints.directions: Continue up Trail No. 415 to the decaying old cabin standing in the trail at roughly 4.5 to 5 miles. There is no sign; the cabin is the junction. Going straight past it leads to Libby Lake, which is not on this route.

waypoints.name: Base of Hoodoo's boulder field
waypoints.note: Boot path fades crossing scree and lingering snow patches west of the cabin; from here it's choose-your-own-line up loose talus to gain the ridge — no defined tread.
waypoints.directions: Take the faint boot path leaving to the right of the cabin into open forest. It gives out in a large clearing, from which the ridge is visible to the north; cross scree and lingering snow patches to the foot of the boulder field.

waypoints.name: Hoodoo Peak
waypoints.note: Class 2 boulder scramble along the summit ridge to the register; many blocks are unstable, test holds before weighting them.
waypoints.directions: There is no defined line and no cairns: pick a way up the loose boulder field to gain the ridge crest, then follow the crest north, boulder-hopping on Class 2 ground with an occasional Class 3 move. Traverse climber's right of the summit spire and hook around it rather than climbing it head on. Test blocks before weighting them.

approach: From the Libby Lake Trailhead (a.k.a. Libby Creek Trailhead, ~4,430 ft; no parking fee or pass required at this trailhead) at the end of Libby Creek Road, follow Libby Creek Trail No. 415 southwest into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail climbs gradually through mixed conifer forest and crosses several tributaries of Libby Creek on logs or hoppable rocks (trekking poles help); tread can be brushy/overgrown in the lower stretches. The first reliable water is North Fork Libby Creek at roughly 3 miles. At about 5 miles you reach a decaying historic line cabin in a clearing — the key junction on this route: continuing straight/west climbs a final steep half-mile (~470 ft) to Libby Lake (7,740 ft), a common basecamp and especially scenic in larch season (late Sept–early Oct), while the right-hand fork is the climbers' route toward Hoodoo. The route does not go to Libby Lake: take the faint boot path to the right of the cabin into open forest, then pick a line up the boulder field and loose gully to the pass on the ridge south of the summit. Once off-trail there is no maintained tread and the boulder field has no single obvious line, so route-finding care is needed — this is the route's main hazard, especially in fog or flat light. From the ridge crest, turn north and follow it over a broad boulder field to the summit; the final stretch is continuous class 2 boulder-hopping with occasional class 3 moves, and loose rock is common, so test holds before weighting them. Snow can linger in the ascent gully and on the upper ridge into June, so carry an ice axe (crampons recommended) for May–June attempts.
